data.title: Impetigo — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Impetigo** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define impetigo. Who gets it?**
- Highly contagious superficial bacterial infection confined to the epidermis (subcorneal), leaving no scar
- Mostly children 2–5 years; spreads in crowded, hot-humid settings, poor hygiene, schools/hostels; in adults usually secondary to another dermatosis

**Q2. Classify pyodermas (a common theory question). Where does impetigo fit?**
- By depth: epidermal — impetigo (non-bullous, bullous); follicular — superficial folliculitis (Bockhart's), sycosis, furuncle, carbuncle; dermal/subcutaneous — ecthyma, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis
- By origin: primary (on normal skin) vs secondary (impetiginisation of eczema, scabies, pediculosis, insect bite, varicella)
- Toxin-mediated: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), toxic shock syndrome, scarlet fever

**Q3. Name the two clinical types and their organisms.**
- Non-bullous (impetigo contagiosa, ~70%): S. aureus is now commonest; Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) alone or together
- Bullous: almost always S. aureus phage group II (commonly type 71) making exfoliative toxins A and B

**Q4. Describe the lesion of non-bullous impetigo.**
- Thin-walled vesicle/pustule on a red base → ruptures quickly → golden-yellow ('honey-coloured') crusts of dried serum
- Face (around nose, mouth) and limbs; satellite lesions by autoinoculation; regional lymphadenopathy common; mild or no itch
- Heals without scarring in 2–3 weeks; may leave transient hypo/hyperpigmentation

**Q5. Describe bullous impetigo.**
- Flaccid, clear-to-turbid bullae 1–2 cm with little surrounding erythema; rupture to leave a thin varnish-like crust with a collarette of scale
- Sites: face, trunk, flexures, napkin area; neonates (formerly 'pemphigus neonatorum')
- No lymphadenopathy usually; localised form of the same toxin disease as SSSS

**Q6. Where is the split in bullous impetigo, and what is the mechanism?**
- Subcorneal / granular layer
- Exfoliative toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein 1 — same target antigen as pemphigus foliaceus and SSSS
- Toxin is local in impetigo (organisms present in the blister); in SSSS it circulates (blister sterile)

**Q7. Why does impetigo stay superficial while SSSS spreads?**
- In SSSS the toxin is absorbed and circulates; babies and adults with renal failure clear it poorly → widespread split at the same level
- Antibodies to the toxin (present in most older children/adults) neutralise it

**Q8. What is the histopathology?**
- Subcorneal pustule/bulla containing neutrophils and Gram-positive cocci; occasional acantholytic cells
- Mild spongiosis; upper dermal neutrophilic infiltrate

**Q9. How will you investigate?**
- Usually a clinical diagnosis
- Gram stain of blister fluid/crust (Gram-positive cocci in clusters/chains); culture and sensitivity if extensive, recurrent, not responding, or MRSA suspected
- Nasal swab for carriage in recurrent cases; urine for haematuria/proteinuria if post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is suspected; ASO titre (often low after skin infection) — anti-DNase B is better

**Q10. Give the differential diagnosis.**
- Non-bullous: herpes simplex / eczema herpeticum (punched-out erosions, grouped), impetiginised atopic or seborrhoeic dermatitis, tinea faciei, scabies with secondary infection, pemphigus foliaceus, discoid eczema
- Bullous: bullous insect-bite reaction, chronic bullous disease of childhood, bullous fixed drug eruption, thermal burn, bullous pemphigoid (adult), SSSS, bullous erythema multiforme, epidermolysis bullosa

**Q11. What are the complications?**
- Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (nephritogenic strains; not prevented by antibiotics) — 1–2 weeks to 1 month later
- Rheumatic fever is NOT a recognised sequel of skin streptococcal infection
- Ecthyma, cellulitis, lymphangitis, bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis; SSSS from bullous strains; scarlet fever; guttate psoriasis
- Psychosocial: school exclusion

**Q12. Outline management.**
- General: gentle removal of crusts with saline/soap-water soaks, separate towels, nail hygiene, keep child off school until 24–48 h of treatment or crusts dry
- Localised: topical mupirocin 2% or fusidic acid 2% (or retapamulin 1%, ozenoxacin 1%) 2–3 times daily for 5–7 days
- Extensive, bullous, systemic features, or failure: oral antibiotics 7 days — cloxacillin/flucloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate; erythromycin/azithromycin if penicillin allergy; MRSA — doxycycline (>8 y), clindamycin, cotrimoxazole, linezolid
- Treat underlying dermatosis; decolonise recurrent carriers (nasal mupirocin, chlorhexidine washes)

**Q13. Why limit use of topical fusidic acid and mupirocin?**
- Resistance develops quickly with long or repeated use
- Use for short courses only; prefer antiseptics (povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, hydrogen peroxide cream) for prevention

**Q14. What is 'impetigo of Bockhart'?**
- Not true impetigo — it is superficial follicular pustules (superficial folliculitis) of S. aureus

**Q15. What is common impetigo variant 'circinate impetigo'?**
- Lesions clear centrally and spread at the edge to form rings — may be mistaken for tinea

**Q16. Topical antibiotics in dermatology — classify (asked as a short note).**
- Mupirocin (inhibits isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase), fusidic acid (blocks elongation factor G), retapamulin (pleuromutilin, 50S), ozenoxacin (quinolone), neomycin + bacitracin + polymyxin (high contact-allergy risk with neomycin), gentamicin, nadifloxacin, clindamycin and erythromycin (acne), metronidazole (rosacea), silver sulfadiazine (burns), sodium fusidate

## Quick spotter facts
- Honey-coloured crust = non-bullous impetigo
- Desmoglein 1 split — bullous impetigo, SSSS, pemphigus foliaceus
- Skin strep → glomerulonephritis, not rheumatic fever

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
